assessment.1. Interference with freedom of expressi: There was a clear interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression: disciplinary proceedings were opened ex officio because of two Facebook posts, and he was ultimately sanctioned with a 5% salary reduction for two months, expressly to deter similar future speech (see paragraphs 16, 20, 24, 26). The measure was capable of producing a chilling effect, all the more so because a disciplinary sanction could also affect future career prospects under domestic law (see paragraph 43, Article 44).

assessment.2. Context of the speech and level of pr: The speech concerned democracy, the rule of law, State institutions and reforms affecting the justice system, that is, matters of obvious public interest (see paragraphs 17-19, 21, 23). The applicant was a serving judge and therefore owed duties of restraint, discretion and impartiality; however, judges also enjoy Article 10 protection, and interferences with their speech call for close scrutiny, especially where they speak on the functioning of justice or the constitutional order (see no. 28396/95; see no. 29492/05). The margin of appreciation is therefore not broad here.

assessment.3. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference had a domestic legal basis in Articles 90, 99(a) and 100 of Law no. 303/2004 (see paragraph 43). It also pursued legitimate aims under Article 10 § 2, namely maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary and protecting the reputation of the justice system (see paragraphs 27, 33-35). That said, the quality of the law was open to doubt: the domestic courts themselves stressed that notions such as the ‘image of the justice system’ were ‘complex and dynamic’ and impossible to define precisely, and practice appears uneven (see paragraphs 40, 49, 51-56). This raises foreseeability concerns under the Court’s quality-of-law approach (see no. 75909/01). Even assuming the measure was prescribed by law, the decisive issue is necessity and proportionality.

assessment.4. Contribution to a debate of public in: Both posts formed part of an ongoing public debate. The first referred to alleged attacks on core State institutions and to the constitutional role of the army in preserving constitutional democracy, in the context of a real institutional dispute concerning the Army Chief of Staff’s term of office (see paragraphs 17-18, 23). The second supported a prosecutor publicly criticising legislative reform and the treatment of judges and prosecutors (see paragraph 19). Neither post concerned a pending case before the applicant, disclosed confidential information, or commented on the merits of judicial proceedings in breach of Article 10 of Law no. 303/2004 (see paragraph 43). This strongly weighs in favour of protection.

assessment.5. Nature of the statements and the dome: The domestic bodies treated the posts largely as improper or defamatory allegations, but that characterization appears unconvincing. The first post was plainly rhetorical and opinion-based; the second was a colloquial expression of support for another magistrate. They were value judgments, or at least mixed statements of opinion and fact, not straightforward factual accusations (see paragraphs 17, 19, 28). Yet the High Court went so far as to say that the truthfulness or factual basis of the statements could not be examined in disciplinary proceedings (see paragraph 38). That approach sits poorly with the Article 10 requirement to assess context, the distinction between fact and value judgment, and the sufficiency of the factual basis. The domestic courts also relied heavily on media headlines, readers’ comments and possible public reactions, rather than on the actual meaning of the applicant’s words (see paragraphs 29, 37, 39). Those reasons do not appear sufficiently relevant and sufficient.

assessment.6. Balance between judicial restraint an: The applicant’s status as a judge and his very large audience on Facebook justified requiring moderation (see paragraphs 16, 23, 39). However, the Court’s case-law accepts that judges may speak out on issues affecting democracy and the judiciary, and even intemperate or provocative language does not automatically justify discipline where the speech contributes to public debate (see no. 28396/95; see no. 29492/05). Here, the applicant spoke in his own name, on issues of institutional importance, and there is no concrete indication that his statements compromised any case, litigant or adjudicatory function. The finding that the posts impaired the image of the justice system remained abstract; the authorities refused the applicant’s request to test that assertion through evidence, while simultaneously inferring damage from media controversy alone (see paragraphs 21-22, 39-40).

assessment.7. Proportionality of the sanction and o: Although the salary reduction was relatively modest in amount, it was still a disciplinary penalty intended to deter future expression, and it was imposed in a context where disciplinary investigations against judges critical of rule-of-law issues had already raised concerns (see paragraphs 26, 71-72). Given the high public-interest value of the speech, the absence of any link to pending cases, the inadequate Convention-based balancing by the domestic courts, and the risk of chilling other judges from participating in public debate, the interference was not shown to answer a pressing social need. The better prediction is therefore that the Court would find a violation of Article 10.
